query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Degradation in additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy is governed by the formation and stability of an Al/Cr-rich oxide scale, whose integrity is compromised under differing gas atmospheres. In oxidizing environments, a continuous, adherent oxide scale forms and protects the alloy, but any process‐induced heterogeneity (e.g., related to additive manufacturing defects) or compositional imbalance (notably in Al/Cr levels) can induce stress concentrations and scale spallation that trigger catastrophic failure. In reducing environments, the destabilization or reduction of this protective oxide layer accelerates void formation and internal degradation, further predisposing the material to rapid failure.
generation.material_initial_state: As-fabricated additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an FCC matrix, exhibiting typical process-induced microstructural heterogeneity and a baseline alloy composition that forms a moderately protective oxide scale on exposure.
generation.intervention: A controlled alteration of the alloy composition – for example, increasing the Al content slightly – to enhance the formation and stability of the Al/Cr-rich oxide scale.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature exposures (e.g., temperatures above 600°C) in controlled oxidizing and reducing gas atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: The oxide scale morphology, in terms of its continuity, thickness, and adhesion to the underlying FCC matrix, mediating local stress fields and interfacial integrity.
generation.mechanism: In an oxidizing atmosphere, the modified alloy (with increased Al content) is expected to form a more robust, adherent Al2O3/Cr2O3 scale that resists deformation and spallation. However, exposure to reducing gases disrupts the stability of this oxide, leading to internal void formation and stress concentration zones which promote crack propagation and catastrophic failure. Process-induced heterogeneities further accentuate these local effects.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy, the modified alloy with augmented Al will exhibit slower degradation and delayed failure in oxidizing conditions due to a more protective oxide layer, while in reducing conditions both alloys may show accelerated degradation; yet, the baseline alloy is predicted to fail catastrophically earlier as its oxide scale is less robust and more sensitive to imperfections.
generation.baseline: The as-fabricated composition and microstructure of Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 without compositional modification, which forms a moderately protective oxide under oxidizing conditions and degrades under reducing conditions with earlier catastrophic failure.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies at elevated temperatures (above ~600°C) and under gas atmospheres that are either strongly oxidizing (high oxygen partial pressure) or reducing (e.g., containing hydrogen or carbon monoxide), where oxide scale formation/demise is the dominant degradation process.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative differences in degradation rates and the critical thresholds for catastrophic failure in each atmosphere remain uncertain due to possible variations in additive manufacturing microstructure and unquantified effects of other elements (such as Ti content) on scale adhesion.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one with the baseline composition and one with a slightly increased Al content. Expose both sets to controlled elevated temperatures (e.g., 650°C) separately in well-characterized oxidizing and reducing atmospheres over a set duration. Characterize the surface oxide scale development, measure crack density, adherence, and monitor time-to-failure or onset of catastrophic degradation.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and continuity (via SEM and TEM)
Adhesion strength of the oxide scale (via scratch tests or indentation methods)
Time-to-initiation of cracking and failure (via in situ high-temperature mechanical testing)
Microstructural changes in the underlying FCC matrix (via XRD and EBSD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy (with higher Al content) does not show a statistically significant improvement in oxide scale stability or delayed onset of catastrophic failure in oxidizing conditions, or if the degradation behaviors under reducing conditions are not measurably different between the two compositions, then the hypothesis that the oxide scale stability driven by Al/Cr content governs degradation and catastrophic failure will be falsified.

chosen.approach: Alloy composition and processing modifications to control degradation
